description: Fifteen visual styles the ui-designer chooses between. The style is DERIVED from the product's domain, audience and job - never asked, never picked by taste. design.json answers what the palette is; this answers what the interface feels like and how it is built. Every entry carries the recipe that makes it convincing, the accessibility cost it imposes, and - the part usually missing - the conditions under which it is the wrong answer.

selection.instruction: Run this before any component is written, in the ui-design phase. Announce the bound style and the one-line reason in the same line as the palette. Never present all fifteen to the user.
inputs: Domain, from design.json signals found in the repo and the request.
Audience: consumer / professional-daily-driver / developer / child / mixed-public.
Session length: glanceable, task-length, or all-day. All-day use rules out every high-stimulus style.
Task stakes: is a mistake expensive (money, health, irreversible) or cheap?
An existing design system or brand. If one exists it WINS - extend it, do not restyle.
Explicit user direction. If the user names a style, that is the binding, and you note any accessibility cost rather than refusing.
scoring: +3 the style's domain_fit.strong contains the detected domain
-99 domain_fit.never contains it - a hard exclusion, not a penalty
-3 the product is an all-day professional tool and the style is high-stimulus
-3 the task stakes are high and the style weakens affordance or contrast
+2 the audience is consumer or brand-led and the style carries personality
+1 the repo already leans this way (rounded tokens, dark-first palette, mono type)
selection.rule: Bind the highest scorer. If two are within 1 point AND would produce materially different interfaces, ask the user once, showing both with their trade-offs - that is a genuine two-option choice, which the Asking Contract permits. Otherwise decide and state the reason.
selection.default: When signals are weak or the domain is generic, bind `minimalism`. It is the style that costs the least when it is wrong.
selection.announce: Style: neo-brutalism (developer tool, brand-led, signals not-enterprise). Palette: devtools, OKLCH, contrast verified.

styles.label: Minimalism
styles.one_line: Space, scale and type carry the hierarchy; nothing decorative survives.
signature: Whitespace as a structural tool, not leftover margin - it separates content, lowers cognitive load and walks the eye to the action
Hierarchy from scale and weight rather than colour or imagery
Bold expressive typography doing the work heavy imagery used to
A small palette: one neutral ramp, one accent, nothing else
Flat colour and clean geometry - restraint, not absence of depth

recipe.spacing: One scale, used consistently. Section rhythm at the top of the scale; component rhythm at the bottom.
recipe.type: A large step between heading and body - 48-64px next to 16px does the work a divider would.
recipe.colour: Neutral surfaces, a single accent reserved for the primary action on each screen.
recipe.depth: Borders and spacing before shadows. A shadow is a last resort, not a default.

use_when: Content or data is the product
All-day professional use
The brand has no strong visual language and should not invent one
avoid_when: The product's job is to be memorable
A crowded market where undifferentiated means invisible
accessibility: The usual failure is low-contrast grey-on-grey passed off as restraint. Verify every pair: 4.5:1 body, 3:1 interactive boundaries.
Removing borders from inputs removes their affordance. Keep a visible boundary on every control.

styles.label: Maximalism
styles.one_line: Deliberate abundance - layered colour, texture, type and imagery, curated rather than chaotic.
signature: Layered colour, texture, typography and imagery building one immersive composition
Exaggerated hierarchy: dramatically oversized type beside very small text, the big type anchoring and the small type rewarding
Oversized sans-serifs, 3D letterforms, wavy or distorted characters
Unusual colour blends and unexpected placement

recipe.structure: A strict underlying grid is what stops abundance becoming noise. The grid is invisible; without it the page is illegible.
recipe.type: Two extremes and nothing between - a display face at 96px+ and body at 16-18px.
recipe.colour: Three to five saturated hues plus a neutral the eye can rest on. Every screen needs one quiet region.
recipe.restraint: One area of the page stays deliberately empty. That emptiness is what makes the rest read as intentional.

use_when: The brand is the product
Campaign, launch and landing pages
Fashion, music, events, creative agencies
avoid_when: Any all-day tool
High-stakes or high-anxiety tasks
Dense data or long forms
accessibility: Text over imagery or gradient needs a scrim or a solid plate - never rely on the image staying dark.
Motion-heavy layering must honour prefers-reduced-motion by reducing movement, not by removing feedback.
Keep one uncluttered reading column; abundance around it is fine, inside it is not.

styles.label: Glassmorphism
styles.one_line: Frosted translucent surfaces floating over a coloured or image background.
signature: backdrop-filter blur with a semi-transparent fill and a light 1px border
A background with enough colour variation that the blur has something to do
Layered panels reading as depth without heavy shadow

recipe.css: background: rgba(255,255,255,0.12); backdrop-filter: blur(12px); -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(12px); border: 1px solid rgba(255,255,255,0.18); border-radius: 16px;
recipe.blur: 8-15px. Cost rises sharply above that and the effect does not improve.
recipe.fallback: Always wrap in @supports (backdrop-filter: blur(1px)); the fallback is a solid, readable surface - not a transparent one.
recipe.performance: At most 2-3 glass elements per viewport, 6-8px blur on mobile. Never animate a backdrop-filtered element; promote with transform: translateZ(0) where it helps.

use_when: A rich background image or gradient is already part of the design
Overlays, modals, navigation bars, media players
Spatial or depth-carrying interfaces
avoid_when: Dense data tables and long forms
Low-end device targets
Any screen where the background is plain - the effect has nothing to blur and reads as a mistake
accessibility: This is the style's real cost: text over translucency can fail contrast depending on what scrolls underneath. Put a semi-opaque plate behind text so contrast is guaranteed regardless of background.
Verify text contrast against the WORST background the panel can sit over, not the screenshot you designed with. Aim high - 7:1 where the content matters.
Keep borders visible; a glass panel with no border loses its edge on light backgrounds.

token_bias.palette: needs a vivid or photographic ground

styles.label: Neumorphism (soft UI)
styles.one_line: Controls extruded from or pressed into a single-colour surface by paired light and dark shadows.
signature: Two box-shadows - one light, one dark - on an element whose background matches its parent
Inset shadow for the pressed state, mimicking a carved surface
A single monochrome base with almost no colour

recipe.pressed: Swap both shadows to inset. The transition should be fast - this is a physical metaphor and lag breaks it.
recipe.light_source: One direction for the whole interface. Two light sources is the tell of a cargo-culted implementation.

use_when: Toggles, sliders and dials - where the carved-out metaphor genuinely helps
Music players, smart-home and simple finance dashboards
Small, sparse control surfaces
avoid_when: Dense SaaS interfaces
E-commerce grids
Anything with many controls per screen
Any product with a broad public audience
accessibility: The defining feature IS the accessibility failure: an element the same colour as its background has no contrast at its boundary. The control's edge is invisible to low-vision users and to everyone in bright sunlight.
Mitigate or do not ship it: add a real border or a contrasting label to every control, plus a high-contrast focus outline. If the mitigation removes the look, the style was wrong for this product.
Text on a shadowed gradient surface is hard to read - keep type off the extruded surface where possible.
Low-relief targets demand precision, which penalises users with motor impairments. Keep hit areas at least 44x44px regardless of the visual size.
styles.caution: Never bind this by default. It requires a deliberate reason and an accessibility mitigation plan stated up front.

styles.label: Claymorphism
styles.one_line: Soft inflated shapes that look like rounded blobs of modelling clay.
signature: Very large border radius, roughly 20-40px
One box-shadow carrying three layers: a big soft outer shadow that lifts the element, an inset shadow away from the light for volume, an inset highlight on the lit side
Pastel and vivid hues together, with soft gradients

recipe.css: border-radius: 32px; background: #f0a6ca; box-shadow: 0 16px 32px rgba(0,0,0,0.12), inset -8px -8px 16px rgba(0,0,0,0.10), inset 8px 8px 16px rgba(255,255,255,0.55);
recipe.note: Unlike neumorphism the element is a different colour from its background - which is exactly why it keeps its contrast and its affordance.

use_when: Onboarding and empty states
Children's and education apps
Friendly consumer fintech
3D landing pages
avoid_when: Dense professional tools
Serious or high-stakes contexts where playful reads as unsafe
accessibility: Safer than neumorphism because the surface differs from the background - but still verify text on pastel fills, which fail contrast easily.
Large radii shrink the usable corner area; keep hit targets generous.

styles.label: Brutalism
styles.one_line: Raw HTML honesty - default elements, system type, almost no styling.
signature: Honesty of materials: the page shows what the web is - HTML, a little CSS, basic controls
Monospace or system fonts, unstyled or barely styled buttons and inputs
Black, white and greys; colour used sparingly if at all
Structure visible rather than hidden under framework chrome

recipe.approach: Start from the browser default stylesheet and resist overriding it. Set a readable measure and line height, and stop.
recipe.performance: Few assets, few computed styles, a short critical rendering path. The speed is not incidental - it is most of the argument.

use_when: Independent, experimental or artist-led projects
Documentation and text-first sites
An audience that reads authenticity as a value
Where maintenance cost and speed matter more than polish
avoid_when: Conversion-critical funnels - excellent for recall, poor for task completion
Any audience expecting conventional affordances
Products where trust is signalled visually, such as payments or healthcare
accessibility: Often accidentally strong: native elements carry correct semantics and keyboard behaviour for free.
The risks are a measure that runs the full window width, and removed focus styles. Cap the measure at 60-75 characters and keep :focus-visible.

styles.label: Neo-brutalism
styles.one_line: Thick black borders, hard zero-blur offset shadows, flat saturated fills.
signature: Borders of roughly 2-5px, usually near-black
Hard offset shadows with zero blur and zero spread - a solid block of colour behind the element
Flat single-colour fills: yellow, lime, cyan, hot pink
Black and white base with one or two extremely saturated accents

recipe.press: On active, translate the element by exactly the shadow offset and remove the shadow - translate(6px, 6px). A mismatch between the two is the most common tell of a cargo-culted implementation.
recipe.three_rules: Zero blur on every shadow. Press distance equal to the shadow offset. An explicit :focus-visible style, since the border alone will not read as focus.

use_when: Creator tools and consumer brands aimed at a younger audience
Launch and campaign pages, portfolios
Developer tooling that wants to signal it is not enterprise software
avoid_when: Enterprise administration
Long-session data work - the high contrast tires at length
Conservative or regulated audiences
accessibility: Usually strong on contrast, which is a real advantage over the soft styles.
The saturated fills must still be checked against their text - yellow with white text fails badly.
Because everything already has a heavy border, focus needs a distinct treatment: an offset outline in a different colour, never a thicker border.

styles.label: Skeuomorphism
styles.one_line: Real-world material and control metaphors, used where the metaphor teaches something.
signature: Material texture - wood, metal, paper, glass - and physical control shapes
Depth and lighting that communicate dimensionality rather than decorate
Controls that look like the thing they emulate: knobs, faders, switches

recipe.principle: The 2026 form is selective, not the 2010 form. Reintroduce depth, texture and metaphor ONLY where they communicate something a flat control could not - never as decoration.
recipe.technique: Layered gradients for curvature, a consistent single light source, texture at low opacity, and a real pressed state with both a visual and a motion response.

use_when: VR, AR and spatial interfaces, where flat surfaces are genuinely confusing
Children's educational apps, where a familiar object lowers cognitive load
Creative tools emulating hardware - audio production, cameras, instruments
avoid_when: General-purpose applications - heavy, slow and dated outside its niches
Anything needing dense information display
accessibility: Textured backgrounds under text are the main hazard; put type on a flat plate.
A realistic knob is often not keyboard-operable. Every emulated control needs a real input underneath it, with arrow-key support and an accessible name.

styles.label: Flat design 2.0
styles.one_line: Flat colour and clean geometry, with just enough shadow and state change to keep affordance.
signature: Solid fills, no gradients or texture for their own sake
Subtle shadows, highlights and layering added back specifically so controls read as controls
Colour shifts on interactive states rather than skeuomorphic feedback

recipe.history: Pure flat design removed the cues that told users what was clickable. Flat 2.0 exists because of that usability failure - it keeps the aesthetic and returns the affordance.
recipe.css: A one- or two-step elevation scale, a clear hover and active colour shift, and a visible border on every input.

use_when: Content-forward interfaces - editorial sites, portfolios, dashboards, landing pages - where the visual system should recede
Broad device and performance range
A brand with its own strong colour that the UI should not compete with
avoid_when: Interaction-heavy applications needing constant feedback - Material is the better answer there
accessibility: The classic flat failure is a button indistinguishable from text. Every actionable element needs at least two of: contrasting fill, border, elevation.
Never signal state with colour alone.

styles.label: Material Design 3 (Expressive)
styles.one_line: A complete token-driven system where shadow, shape and motion are the feedback language.
signature: Design tokens named by purpose rather than appearance - colour, type, spacing, shape
Shape tokens as a named scale (none, extra-small, small, medium, large, extra-large, full) rather than hard-coded radii
Deep tonal palettes generated from a source colour; dynamic theming
Motion as feedback: elevation change, shape morphing, and variable-font axes carrying expression

recipe.approach: Adopt the system, do not imitate its look. The value is the token layer and the component contracts; a hand-rolled Material lookalike takes the visual cost with none of the consistency benefit.
recipe.tooling: Generate the theme from a brand colour with the Material Theme Builder and export tokens; wire components to tokens, never to literals.

use_when: Android, or a cross-platform product that should feel native on Android
Interaction-heavy applications where users need continuous feedback about what is draggable, dismissible or clickable
Large teams needing an off-the-shelf system with documented component behaviour
avoid_when: A brand with a strong visual identity of its own - Material will dominate it
iOS-only products, where it reads as foreign
Small static or content sites, where the system is far more machinery than the job needs
accessibility: Strong by default: the tonal palette is generated to hit contrast targets, and components ship with correct roles and states.
The failure mode is overriding tokens with literals, which quietly breaks the guarantees. Hard-coded hex values inside Material components mean the system is no longer doing its job.

styles.label: Bento UI
styles.one_line: A modular grid of tiles of deliberately unequal size, where size encodes priority.
signature: Tiles of different spans in one grid, breaking the monotony of an equal-cell layout
Larger tiles for priority content creating natural focal points; smaller tiles supporting them
Each tile a self-contained unit that can stand alone or combine
Generous, consistent gutters - crowding is what makes a bento layout fail

recipe.css: display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(12, 1fr); gap: 16px; with tiles spanning 4/6/8 columns and 1-2 rows.
recipe.hierarchy: Decide what matters most FIRST, then assign spans. A bento grid whose tile sizes do not encode importance is just an uneven layout.
recipe.content: One idea per tile. Overstuffing a tile removes the clarity the format exists to provide.
recipe.responsive: Collapse to a single column on mobile in priority order - largest tile first. The layout must not depend on a two-dimensional reading order.

use_when: Feature overviews and product landing pages
Dashboards with metrics of genuinely different importance
Portfolio and showcase pages
Anywhere a summary must be scannable at a glance
avoid_when: Uniform lists - a catalogue of equal items should be an equal grid
Long-form reading
Dense tabular data
accessibility: DOM order must match visual priority, or keyboard and screen-reader users get the layout in a meaningless sequence. Never reorder with grid placement alone.
Each tile needs a real heading so the page outline is navigable.
A tile that is entirely clickable still needs one focusable element with an accessible name - not a click handler on a div.
styles.note: Bento is a LAYOUT, not a skin. It composes with almost any other style - minimalism, glass, neo-brutalism - and is usually bound alongside one rather than instead of one.

styles.label: Y2K
styles.one_line: Late-90s digital optimism: chrome, iridescence, bubble letterforms and cyber grids.
signature: Chrome and liquid-metal type - the single most recognisable element
Inflated bubble letterforms
Cyber grids and wireframe perspective
Neon-to-pastel gradient blobs, pixel and bitmap texture, glitch and scan-line distortion

recipe.chrome: Dark or neutral ground, then a gradient moving between two or three iridescent colours, then a soft highlight on top to mimic light hitting the surface. Apply to bold rounded letterforms with background-clip: text.
recipe.surfaces: Rounded cards with subtle glossy inner shadows.
recipe.palette: Chrome silver as the structural surface; bubblegum pink and lime green as emotional accents; frosted aqua and cyber navy for depth; a holographic gradient for the signature pearl reflectance.

use_when: Fashion, music, gaming and youth-culture brands
Campaign and event microsites
Products whose audience has genuine nostalgia for the era
avoid_when: Any professional tool
Audiences outside the nostalgia window, to whom it reads as unserious rather than knowing
accessibility: Chrome gradient text is often unreadable at body size - use it for display only, and keep body copy in a flat, high-contrast colour.
Glitch and scan-line animation must be gated behind prefers-reduced-motion; these effects can trigger discomfort.
Never put essential information in a gradient-filled or distorted element.

styles.label: Retro / vintage
styles.one_line: One specific decade, committed to consistently across colour, type and ornament.
signature: A chosen era, followed properly - 1970s earth tones (mustard, burnt orange, avocado, chocolate), 1980s neon (hot pink, teal, purple, lime), 1990s softs (lavender, sage, dusty rose, cream)
Period-appropriate display type - bold decorative for the 70s, pixel faces for the 80s
Muted, less saturated colour for authenticity - period printing could not produce today's gamut
Grain, halftone and print texture

recipe.rule: Pick one decade and hold to it. Mixing eras is what makes retro read as generic rather than deliberate.
recipe.type: Decorative faces for headlines only; clean, readable body type underneath. Period charm must not reach the paragraph.
recipe.texture: A low-opacity grain overlay does most of the work of making flat colour feel printed.

use_when: Food, drink and hospitality brands
Music, film and event products
Heritage brands with a real history to reference
avoid_when: Products whose value proposition is being current
Complex applications - the ornament competes with the interface
accessibility: Muted period palettes fail contrast easily. Keep the period hues for surfaces and ornament, and darken text beyond what the era used.
Decorative and pixel faces are poor at small sizes - never below 18px, and never for body copy.
Grain overlays must sit behind text, never over it.

styles.label: Cyberpunk
styles.one_line: Near-black ground, restrained neon accents, terminal typography and HUD framing.
signature: Absolute black or deep charcoal ground with neon accents covering no more than 10-15% of the surface
Acid yellow, cyan and hot pink as the accent set
Monospace code faces - JetBrains Mono, Fira Code, IBM Plex Mono - with all-caps labels and fixed-width layout
Scan lines, chromatic aberration and glitch animation suggesting lived-in, imperfect technology

recipe.restraint: One loud focal element per page - a cyan border with glow. Everything else uses quiet borders. Neon everywhere is neon nowhere, and it becomes unreadable.
recipe.glow: A layered box-shadow in the accent hue at low alpha, not a filter - filters are far more expensive and blur the edge you want crisp.
recipe.text: Body text around rgba(255,255,255,0.55) on a #05050a ground passes AA. Do not drop text opacity below 0.45.

use_when: Developer tools, security and infrastructure products
Gaming and esports
Crypto and trading interfaces where a dark room is the real usage context
avoid_when: All-day productivity tools - neon-on-dark causes eye strain over long sessions
Audiences with mixed or unknown accessibility needs
Bright-environment usage, where a pure-black UI is hard to read
accessibility: Pure black with pure neon is the maximum-eye-strain combination. Use a near-black ground (#05050a) rather than #000, and cap accent coverage.
Glitch and scan-line effects must be gated behind prefers-reduced-motion - show the static version.
Monospace all-caps hurts scanning at length; use it for labels and data, not for prose.
Offer a light theme unless the product is genuinely dark-only.

styles.label: Editorial
styles.one_line: Magazine discipline: a real grid, typographic hierarchy, and white space doing structural work.
signature: A column grid as the primary tool - six to eight columns at desktop, collapsing cleanly
Hierarchy from type scale rather than colour: a 64px headline beside 16px body creates its own structure
Generous margins and white space that moves the reader and slows the eye
Consistency of fonts, colours and spacing across every article template

recipe.measure: 50-75 characters per line. The single highest-impact readability decision on a text-led site.
recipe.type: Body at 16px minimum on web; leading at 120-150% of the font size.
recipe.grid: Define the grid first and place images to it - a full-bleed image and a three-column pull quote both read as intentional only if the grid exists beneath them.
recipe.scale: One strong display face and one highly readable text face is enough. A third font is almost always decoration.

use_when: Publications, long-form content, documentation and research
Marketing sites where the argument is the product
Any product where reading time is the core metric
avoid_when: Application interfaces with dense controls
Short transactional flows
accessibility: Usually strong, because the discipline is readability. Keep the measure capped and honour user font-size settings by sizing in rem.
Do not let a decorative drop cap break the reading order for screen readers.
Pull quotes and captions still need to meet contrast - they are the usual offenders, set too light on purpose.

styles.label: Liquid Glass (Apple)
styles.one_line: Apple's system material - translucency that refracts, reacts and adapts to what is behind it.
signature: A rendering model that happens to look glassy, not a glassy look - that distinction is the whole style
Real optical behaviour: reflection, refraction and light interaction, with a sense of fluidity
Adapts in real time to surrounding content, shifting to keep focus on the content rather than the chrome
Applied to controls, navigation bars, tab bars, widgets and icons - the system surfaces, not the content

recipe.native: On Apple platforms use the system material APIs. Do not hand-roll it - the OS version reacts to content, scroll and ambient light in ways CSS cannot reproduce, and a hand-rolled copy will drift from the system every release.
recipe.web: CSS can approximate but not match: layered backdrop-filter with a slight saturate(), a specular highlight along the top edge, and a border that brightens where light would catch. Accept that it is an approximation and say so.
recipe.restraint: Glass is for chrome. Content sits on opaque surfaces - Apple's own apps do this, and skipping it is what makes third-party imitations feel unreadable.

use_when: iOS 26, iPadOS 26, macOS Tahoe, watchOS, tvOS or visionOS products
A cross-platform product that should feel native on Apple hardware
Spatial interfaces where translucency communicates depth
avoid_when: Android-only or web-only products, where it reads as a foreign system's furniture
Any interface whose content is dense text or tabular data
accessibility: Same core hazard as glassmorphism, one layer deeper: contrast depends on what is behind the surface, and here that changes dynamically.
Honour Reduce Transparency and Increase Contrast - on Apple platforms these are system settings the material already responds to, which is another reason to use the system API rather than imitate it.
Never place body text directly on the material.

styles.label: Swiss / International Typographic Style
styles.one_line: The mathematical grid, sans-serif type and objectivity - the movement every 12-column layout descends from.
signature: A modular grid, used strictly, with asymmetric composition inside it
One sans-serif family, left-aligned, ranged left and ragged right
White space as an active element rather than leftover
Objective photography and geometric form; no ornament, no illustration flourish

recipe.grid: Establish the modular grid first and place everything to it, including the exceptions. Asymmetry inside a strict grid is the signature - centring everything is the most common misreading of the style.
recipe.type: One family, two or three sizes, differentiated by weight and position rather than by adding faces. Helvetica, Univers or a modern equivalent.
recipe.hierarchy: Position and scale, never colour. If removing all colour destroys the hierarchy, the layout is not Swiss.

use_when: Institutional, governmental and academic products
Design-literate audiences where restraint reads as competence
Data and wayfinding, which is what the style was invented for
avoid_when: Brands that need warmth or personality
Consumer products competing on emotional appeal
accessibility: Structurally excellent - the grid produces a sane DOM order and the hierarchy survives colour blindness entirely.
The one risk is the authentic ragged-right at very narrow widths; set a sensible minimum column width so lines do not fragment.

styles.label: Spatial / depth-first
styles.one_line: Layering, perspective and real 3D used to solve comprehension - never for the wow.
signature: Depth and layered motion creating hierarchy, so the interface behaves like an environment rather than a flat page
Components with weight: cards that feel stackable, controls that respond with intention
Genuine 3D where two dimensions cannot carry the information - configurators, spatial navigation, dimensional data

recipe.test: The binding question: does the third dimension carry information a 2D version could not? If the answer is no, this is decoration with a loading cost, and the style is wrong.
recipe.tech: WebGPU where supported with a 2D fallback; Spline or Three.js for authored scenes. Budget the payload - a 3D hero that delays first paint has already lost.
recipe.motion: Depth is communicated by parallax and shadow softness, not by spinning things.

use_when: Product configurators and 3D data visualisation
visionOS and spatial-computing targets, where flat surfaces are genuinely confusing
Physical products whose shape is the selling point
avoid_when: Text-led or form-led products
Low-end device targets and constrained bandwidth
Anything where a flat diagram explains it better
accessibility: A 3D canvas is opaque to screen readers. Every spatial view needs an equivalent non-visual path to the same information - not a caption saying a model exists.
Parallax and depth motion are a common vestibular trigger. Gate on prefers-reduced-motion and flatten, do not merely slow.
Keyboard and gaze are different input models - do not assume a pointer.

styles.label: Generative / agentic UI
styles.one_line: The interface is assembled at runtime by an agent from a catalogue of pre-approved components.
signature: A conversational layer OVER a conventional UI - users can click the normal flow or just ask
Structured UI cards: the agent returns real production components with typed arguments, not free-form markup
Visible agent state: what it is doing, why, and an override at every step
Graceful, legible error recovery rather than a failed turn

recipe.spectrum: Three patterns, from tightest to loosest: structured cards (predictable, bounded), component selection from a catalogue, and open-ended surfaces. Most products should mix them by surface area - tight where actions are irreversible, loose where exploration is the point.
recipe.critical_rule: The agent selects from pre-approved components and passes structured arguments. It does NOT emit markup. That boundary is what separates generative UI from a chatbot rendering HTML, and it is the whole safety story.
recipe.conventional_first: Build the conventional UI first. The conversational layer sits on top of it. A product that is only a chat box has removed every affordance the user had.

use_when: AI-assisted products where user intent is too varied for fixed screens
Agentic workflows that take actions on a user's behalf
Data exploration where the useful view differs per question
avoid_when: Irreversible or high-stakes actions without an explicit confirmation step outside the generated surface
Regulated flows that must be identical every time and auditable
accessibility: A runtime-composed surface must still announce itself. Manage focus deliberately on each new surface and use a live region for agent progress, or screen-reader users are told nothing happened.
Never let the agent produce an interactive element that has not been through the component catalogue - accessibility is a property of the catalogue, not of the generation.
Every agent action needs an override and an undo. Autonomy without a stop control is not a design, it is a liability.
styles.note: This is an interaction architecture, not a skin - bind it alongside one, the way bento is bound alongside one.

styles.label: Aurora / mesh gradient
styles.one_line: Blurred radial colour blobs layered over a deep ground, glowing slowly.
signature: Heavily blurred overlapping radial shapes producing organic depth - not a linear gradient
Soft colour blobs over a deep, usually dark background
Glass or solid panels floating above the glow like objects suspended in light
Slow movement: 8-12 second cycles, never frantic colour shifting

recipe.css: Two or three absolutely-positioned radial-gradient layers, each with filter: blur(80px) or more, animated on background-position or transform over 8-12s. Pure CSS - resolution-independent and far lighter than an image.
recipe.restraint: It reads as premium when contextual - a hero breathing slowly, a card edge catching light on hover. Applied to every surface it reads as a template.
recipe.performance: Blur at this radius is expensive. One aurora region per page, and never animate it alongside a backdrop-filtered panel.

use_when: SaaS and AI product landing pages
Creative tools that need to feel alive
Brands positioning against visually conservative competitors
avoid_when: Application interiors - it competes with every piece of data
Low-end devices, where the blur radius is a real cost
accessibility: Text never sits directly on the gradient - it moves, so its contrast against any given word moves with it. Put text on a panel.
Honour prefers-reduced-motion by freezing the animation, keeping the gradient.
styles.note: A background treatment rather than a full skin - it pairs with minimalism, glass or bento.

styles.label: Kinetic typography
styles.one_line: Text that moves to introduce meaning, then settles so it can be read.
signature: Type animated on scroll, timing or interaction - scaling, morphing, revealing
Motion capturing the eye before colour or shape does, pulling attention to the most important words
Variable-font axes animated rather than swapped, which is what made this practical
A stable end state - the animation resolves and stops

recipe.rule: Motion introduces meaning, then settles. If a reader must wait for an animation to finish before they can read, the animation has become a paywall on the content.
recipe.tech: Variable fonts plus a scroll-linked animation; Motion (Framer Motion) in React for scroll reveals; GSAP for sequenced timelines; Lottie only when the effect genuinely cannot be done in CSS.
recipe.scope: Display type only. Body copy never moves.

use_when: Landing and campaign pages where a headline must land
Brand and portfolio sites
Storytelling and scrollytelling formats
avoid_when: Application interfaces
Anything a user reads repeatedly - the animation that delighted once is friction on the fourth visit
accessibility: prefers-reduced-motion must show the final state immediately, not a slower animation.
Text mid-animation can be unreadable and can confuse screen readers if it is split into per-character spans - keep the accessible name intact with aria-label on the whole phrase.
Never animate anything a user must read to complete a task.
styles.note: A motion layer rather than a skin; bind it alongside one.

styles.label: Dark-first data interface
styles.one_line: Near-monochrome dark surfaces where the data is the loudest thing on screen.
signature: Dark by default, light as the second theme - the pattern Linear, Supabase and Vercel established for all-day tools
Radical restraint: near-monochrome panels, one or two accents, everything non-essential absent
Low-contrast panel borders, crisp typography, high information density that does not feel crowded
Keyboard-first interaction - command palette, shortcuts, focus order that makes sense

recipe.type: Slightly bolder and larger than on light: semi-bold or medium, never ultra-thin, which disappears against dark surfaces.
recipe.colour: Two or three accents maximum. In financial contexts tune green and red for dark surfaces, and add a second cue - an arrow or a sign - so the meaning survives colour blindness.
recipe.surfaces: Elevation lightens the surface rather than adding a shadow; a shadow on a dark ground is invisible.

use_when: Monitoring, observability and operations consoles
Overnight shifts and low-light environments
Dense real-time data where extended viewing causes eye strain
Developer tools used all day
avoid_when: Bright-environment or outdoor usage
Long-form reading
Products whose audience has not opted into a dark aesthetic - ship light as a real theme, not an afterthought
accessibility: Dark mode is not inverted light mode. Regenerate the palette: elevation lightens, accents lose chroma, and pure white text on pure black is too harsh - back both off.
Verify contrast on the dark theme independently. A pair that passes on light frequently fails inverted.
Never rely on a status colour alone - dark surfaces compress perceived colour difference further.

default_style.rule: When the domain is generic, the signals are weak, or nothing scores above the others, bind minimalism. It is the declared default and it must remain bindable for EVERY domain - its domain_fit.never is empty by design, and the validator enforces that.
default_style.why: It is the style that costs the least when it is wrong. A minimal interface applied to a product that wanted personality is merely plain; a cyberpunk or maximalist interface applied to a product that wanted calm is actively harmful. When uncertain, the asymmetry of the downside decides.
default_style.not_an_excuse: Defaulting is a real decision and is stated as one - 'minimalism (default: no strong domain signal in this repo)'. Never present it as though the domain demanded it.

anti_patterns.note: Styles that appear in trend lists but should not be bound. Named here so the reasoning is on record rather than rediscovered.
anti_patterns.corporate-memphis: Flat geometric illustration with bendy disproportionate figures in non-representational colours. Widely declared exhausted, and criticised on substance: it strips human individuality into a uniform visual language, and its frictionless-joy imagery reads as evasive on products whose reality is anything but. Do not reach for it as the default illustration style; commission or select imagery that says something specific about this product instead.
anti_patterns.anti-design: Deliberate ugliness - broken grids, clashing colour, mismatched type. Its rebellious edge is real but it is almost never what a client's users need, and neo-brutalism already delivers the personality with the affordances intact. Bind it only when the user explicitly asks for it.
anti_patterns.trend_chasing: A style bound because it is current, with no argument from domain, audience, session length or stakes, is a style that will need replacing when the trend moves. The reason is the deliverable, not the look.

combination_rules.layout_plus_skin: `bento` and `editorial` are layout systems; the other thirteen are skins. One layout plus one skin is a normal, good binding - bento tiles in a minimalist skin, or an editorial grid with neo-brutalist accents.
combination_rules.reason: Each of those pairs makes contradictory claims about depth, ornament or restraint. An interface making both claims reads as unfinished rather than as a blend.
combination_rules.one_skin: Exactly one skin per product. A second skin for one screen is how a design system starts dying.

never: Never present the full list of fifteen to the user. Deriving the style from the domain is the job; a menu is the abdication of it.
Never bind a style whose domain_fit marks the detected domain `never`, whatever it looks like.
Never restyle an existing design system. If the repo has one, extend it - the bound style then describes new surfaces only, and that limitation is stated.
Never let a style's accessibility cost go unstated. If a style needs mitigation to be usable, the mitigation ships with it or the style does not.
Never choose by taste or by what is currently fashionable. The reason must be stated in terms of domain, audience, session length or stakes.
